project.title: Does a Q-Tip Actually Clean Your Ears?
project.visual_style: cinematic close-up 3D medical animation, warm coral-pink ear canal tunnel, organic soft tissue folds, glossy amber earwax, white cotton swab, anatomical cutaway, smooth camera journey
project.educational_goal: Explain how earwax forms, how the ear naturally moves it outward, and why cotton swabs can push wax deeper.
source_notes: Earwax is made in the outer part of the ear canal by glands and skin cells.
Earwax helps trap dust and debris and protects the ear canal.
The skin of the ear canal gradually migrates outward, helping move wax toward the opening.
Cotton swabs can push wax deeper into the canal and may injure the ear.

narration_beats.text: Inside your ear, a natural substance called earwax is constantly being made. It helps trap dust and protects the delicate skin of your ear canal.
Your ear canal slowly moves its skin outward, carrying old wax and trapped debris toward the opening. Most of the time, your ears clean themselves.
But pushing a cotton swab into the canal can move wax in the opposite direction, packing it deeper instead of bringing it out.
That is why cotton swabs should not be pushed inside the ear canal. The outer ear is enough for ordinary cleaning.
